extracted.intended_audience: artists, architects, writers, and students of aesthetics/philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative principles for producing the sublime and the beautiful across arts and architecture: which sensory inputs, colours, sounds, proportions, and associations produce grandeur or loveliness, and which do not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of darkness and light contrast to produce the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: Darkness itself ... is known by experience to have a greater effect on the passions than light. To make an object very striking, we should make it as different as possible from the objects with which we have been immediately conversant; when therefore you enter a building, you cannot pass into a greater light than you had in the open air; to go into one some few degrees less luminous, can make only a trifling change; but to make the transition thoroughly striking, you ought to pass from the greatest light, to as much darkness as is consistent with the uses of architecture. At night the contrary rule will hold, but for the very same reason; and the more highly a room is then illuminated, the grander will the passion be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use strong contrast between prior illumination and interior darkness to maximally arouse sublime passions (by surprise and difference). Reverse lighting strategy for night: brighter illumination at night heightens grandeur. Apply as appropriate to the intended effect (not every building should be made melancholy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Colour considered productive of the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: Among colours, such as are soft or cheerful ... are unfit to produce grand images. ... the materials and ornaments ought neither to be white, nor green, nor yellow, nor blue, nor of a pale red, nor violet nor spotted, but of sad and fuscous colours, as black, or brown, or deep purple, and the like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For the 'highest degree of the sublime' prefer melancholy, dark, fuscous colouring (black, brown, deep purple). Avoid gay/gaudy drapery and cheerful/pale colours when aiming for sublime. Much gilding, mosaics, painting, or statues contribute little. This rule is chiefly for producing a uniform, striking sublimity and need not be used where other sources supply grandeur; avoid anything 'light and riant' that deadens the taste for the sublime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sound and loudness as a source of the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: Sounds have a great power ... Excessive loudness alone is sufficient to overpower the soul, to suspend its action, and to fill it with terror. The noise of vast cataracts, raging storms, thunder, or artillery, awakes a great and awful sensation ... The shouting of multitudes has a similar effect; and, by the sole strength of the sound, so amazes and confounds the imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use very loud natural or mechanical sounds (thunder, waterfalls, cannon, mass shouting) to overwhelm and produce awe/terror. The effect arises from force rather than nicety or artifice in the sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suddenness in sound produces the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: A sudden beginning, or sudden cessation, of sound of any considerable force, has the same power. The attention is roused by this; and the faculties driven forward, as it were on their guard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ abrupt onsets or stops of strong sounds to startle and rouse attention. Note that easy transitions between extremes cause no terror and thus cannot produce greatness. Repetition of a single strong short sound at intervals (striking of a great clock, a single stroke on a drum, successive firing of cannon) can have a grand effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermitting (low, tremulous) sounds and uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: A low, tremulous, intermitting sound ... is productive of the sublime. ... some low, confused, uncertain sounds leave us in the same fearful anxiety concerning their causes, that no light, or an uncertain light, does concerning the objects that surround us. A light now appearing, and now leaving us, and so off and on, is even more terrible than total darkness; and a sort of uncertain sounds are, when the necessary dispositions concur, more alarming than a total silence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use intermittent, low, trembling or uncertain sounds to create anxiety and fearful imagination through uncertainty. Pairing uncertain sound with uncertain light increases terror.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural cries (of men and animals) convey the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: Such sounds as imitate the natural inarticulate voices of men, or any animals, in pain or danger, are capable of conveying great ideas; unless it be the well-known voice of some creature, on which we are used to look with contempt. The angry tones of wild beasts are equally capable of causing a great and awful sensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitate or evoke natural, inarticulate cries (pain, danger, wild beasts) to convey greatness and awe; beware that familiar contemptible voices will not have the effect. Natural cries communicate meaning even without prior acquaintance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smell and taste: only extreme bitters and stenches produce sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: Smells and Tastes, have some share too in ideas of greatness; but it is a small one ... no smells or tastes can produce a grand sensation, except excessive bitters, and intolerable stenches. ... when they are moderated, as in a description or narrative, they become sources of the sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only extreme bitter tastes or intolerable stenches can directly invoke sublime sensations; when treated moderately in description or narrative they can function as legitimate sublime images (e.g., Virgil's poisonous exhalations). Avoid unseemly association with mean or contemptible ideas, which degrades the sublime; test sublime images by whether they maintain dignity when united with allowed grandeur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feeling (bodily pain) as a source of the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea of bodily pain, in all the modes and degrees of labour, pain, anguish, torment, is productive of the sublime; and nothing else in this sense can produce it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depicting bodily pain, anguish or torment can produce sublime emotion because the sublime is closely connected to self-preservation and distress. The strongest sublime emotion is one of distress rather than positive pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Beauty (distinguished from the sublime and desire)
rubrics_metrics.description: By beauty I mean that quality, or those qualities in bodies, by which they cause love, or some passion similar to it. ... I likewise distinguish love, by which I mean that satisfaction which arises to the mind upon contemplating anything beautiful, of whatsoever nature it may be, from desire or lust; which is an energy of the mind, that hurries us on to the possession of certain objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat beauty as the sensible qualities that produce an immediate feeling of love/satisfaction on contemplation, not as desire or possession. Confine discussion of beauty to sensible qualities for analytic simplicity; beauty's psychological effect is immediate and not dependent on reasoning or will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion is not the primary cause of beauty (general principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty hath usually been said to consist in certain proportions of parts. ... I have great reason to doubt, whether beauty be at all an idea belonging to proportion. Proportion relates almost wholly to convenience, as every idea of order seems to do; and it must therefore be considered as a creature of the understanding, rather than a primary cause acting on the senses and imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume fixed measurements or mathematical proportions (e.g., seven, eight, ten heads) as the cause of beauty. Beauty is immediate, sensory, and can exist independent of exact mensuration; proportion often belongs more to reason and utility than to the sensory effect that creates beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for testing whether proportion causes beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: (Rules laid down by the author) 1. If two bodies produce the same or a similar effect on the mind, and on examination they are found to agree in some of their properties, and to differ in others; the common effect is to be attributed to the properties in which they agree, and not to those in which they differ. 2. Not to account for the effect of a natural object from the effect of an artificial object. 3. Not to account for the effect of any natural object from a conclusion of our reason concerning its uses, if a natural cause may be assigned. 4. Not to admit any determinate quantity, or any relation of quantity, as the cause of a certain effect, if the effect is produced by different or opposite measures and relations; or if these measures and relations may exist, and yet the effect may not be produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When investigating causes of beauty, favor properties common across similarly effective objects, avoid inferring natural beauty from artificial examples, do not substitute rational conclusions about use for nearer natural causes, and reject a fixed quantitative rule if the effect occurs across diverse measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion is not the cause of beauty in vegetables, animals, or humans (empirical argument)
rubrics_metrics.description: On examining flowers, beasts, birds, and the human species, we find beauty in a vast variety of shapes, colours, and relative measures; some very different or even opposite forms are yet beautiful (rose vs. apple blossom; swan vs. peacock; male vs. female human proportions). Therefore no certain measures operating from a natural principle are necessary to produce beauty; manner rather than measure creates beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empirical observation: beauty appears across widely differing proportions in plants, animals, and humans. Artists should not rely on a single proportional formula; the same proportions occur in both handsome and ugly bodies. Proportion may help define a kind's common form but does not generate the sensory pleasure of beauty itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution against deriving artistic/architectural rules from forced analogies to nature (human figure analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: It appears very clearly to me, that the human figure never supplied the architect with any of his ideas. ... several buildings are by no means of the form of that particular square, which are notwithstanding planned by the best architects, and produce an effect altogether as good, and perhaps a better. ... I am apt to suspect that these analogies were devised to give a credit to the works of art, by showing a conformity between them and the noblest works in nature, not that the latter served at all to supply hints for the perfection of the former.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rigidly copy supposed 'natural' proportions (e.g., man-with-arms-extended square) as the source of architectural excellence. Be wary of projecting artificial measures onto nature; instead evaluate artistic proportions by their own sensory and functional effects rather than forced analogies.
